imo-2008-01.title: The circumcentre is the centre (vectors)
imo-2008-01.body:
Let $O$ be the circumcentre, $R$ the circumradius, and use vectors with origin $O$, so $|A|=|B|=|C|=R$ and the orthocentre is $H=A+B+C$. Let $M_a=\frac{B+C}{2}$ be the midpoint of $BC$.

$A_1,A_2$ lie on line $BC$ at distance $M_aH$ from $M_a$, and $OM_a\perp BC$. By Pythagoras,
$$OA_1^2=OA_2^2=OM_a^2+M_aH^2 .$$
Now $M_aH=H-M_a=A+\frac{B+C}{2}$, so
$$M_aH^2=R^2+A\cdot(B+C)+\frac{|B+C|^2}{4},\qquad OM_a^2=\frac{|B+C|^2}{4},$$
and since $|B+C|^2=2R^2+2B\cdot C$,
$$OA_1^2=R^2+A\cdot B+A\cdot C+\frac{2R^2+2B\cdot C}{2}=2R^2+A\cdot B+B\cdot C+C\cdot A .$$
This expression is symmetric in $A,B,C$, so the same computation gives the same value for $OB_1^2=OB_2^2$ and $OC_1^2=OC_2^2$. Hence all six points lie on the circle with centre $O$ and radius $\sqrt{2R^2+A\cdot B+B\cdot C+C\cdot A}$. ∎

imo-2008-01.title: Radical axes
imo-2008-01.body:
Let $\Gamma_A,\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C$ be the three circles, centred at the midpoints $M_a,M_b,M_c$. The circles $\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C$ both pass through $H$, so their radical axis is the line through $H$ perpendicular to $M_bM_c$. As $M_bM_c\parallel BC$, this is the altitude from $A$, which contains $A$. So $A$ has equal powers: $\overline{AB_1}\cdot\overline{AB_2}=\overline{AC_1}\cdot\overline{AC_2}$ (signed lengths), and by the converse of the power of a point, $B_1,B_2,C_1,C_2$ lie on a circle $\omega_A$. Similarly $C_1,C_2,A_1,A_2$ lie on a circle $\omega_B$ and $A_1,A_2,B_1,B_2$ on a circle $\omega_C$.

If these three circles were pairwise different, their pairwise radical axes would be the lines $B_1B_2=CA$ ($\omega_A,\omega_C$), $C_1C_2=AB$ ($\omega_A,\omega_B$) and $A_1A_2=BC$ ($\omega_B,\omega_C$). By the radical axis theorem these three lines would be concurrent or all parallel, but the sides of a triangle are neither. So two of the circles coincide, and then that circle contains all six points. ∎

imo-2008-02.title: Substitution $a=\frac{x}{x-1}$
imo-2008-02.body:
**(a)** Put $a=\frac{x}{x-1}$, $b=\frac{y}{y-1}$, $c=\frac{z}{z-1}$. These are defined for $x,y,z\ne1$, never equal $1$, and conversely $x=\frac{a}{a-1}$, etc. The condition $xyz=1$ becomes $abc=(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)$, i.e.
$$ab+bc+ca=a+b+c-1 .$$
Therefore
$$a^2+b^2+c^2=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)=(a+b+c)^2-2(a+b+c)+2=(a+b+c-1)^2+1\ge1 .$$

**(b)** Equality holds iff $a+b+c=1$ and then $ab+bc+ca=0$. For a rational $t\ne0,-1$ let $D=t^2+t+1>0$ and
$$a=\frac{-t}{D},\qquad b=\frac{t+1}{D},\qquad c=\frac{t(t+1)}{D}.$$
Then $a+b+c=\frac{t^2+t+1}{D}=1$ and $D^2(ab+bc+ca)=-t(t+1)+t(t+1)^2-t^2(t+1)=t(t+1)\bigl(-1+(t+1)-t\bigr)=0$. Also $a-1=-\frac{(t+1)^2}{D}$, $b-1=-\frac{t^2}{D}$, $c-1=-\frac1D$ are nonzero, so going back,
$$x=\frac{a}{a-1}=\frac{t}{(t+1)^2},\qquad y=\frac{b}{b-1}=-\frac{t+1}{t^2},\qquad z=\frac{c}{c-1}=-t(t+1).$$
These are rational, different from $1$, and $xyz=\frac{t}{(t+1)^2}\cdot\frac{t+1}{t^2}\cdot t(t+1)=1$. Since $z=-t(t+1)$ takes each value for at most two $t$, we get infinitely many triples. (Example: $t=1$ gives $(\frac14,-2,-2)$: $\frac19+\frac49+\frac49=1$.) ∎

imo-2008-03.title: Start from the prime
imo-2008-03.body:
**Primes $\equiv1\pmod 4$.** For such a prime $p$, $-1$ is a quadratic residue (e.g. $\left(\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!\right)^2\equiv-1$ by Wilson's theorem). There are infinitely many such primes: given primes $p_1,\dots,p_r$, any prime factor $q$ of $N=(2p_1\cdots p_r)^2+1$ is odd, different from the $p_i$, and has $-1$ as a quadratic residue, so $x^{q-1}\equiv(-1)^{(q-1)/2}$ for $x=2p_1\cdots p_r$ forces $q\equiv1\pmod4$.

**Construction.** Let $p\equiv1\pmod4$ be a prime with $p\ge29$. Pick $x$ with $x^2\equiv-1\pmod p$, reduce it to $0<x<p$, and replace $x$ by $p-x$ if necessary, to get an integer $n$ with $1\le n<\frac p2$ and $p\mid n^2+1$.

Let $k=p-2n>0$. Then $2n\equiv-k\pmod p$, so $0\equiv4(n^2+1)\equiv k^2+4\pmod p$. As $k^2+4>0$, $k^2+4\ge p$, i.e. $k\ge\sqrt{p-4}\ge5$. Therefore $p-4\ge p-k=2n$, more precisely $p-4>2n$ (since $k\ge5$), and
$$p=2n+k\ge 2n+\sqrt{p-4}>2n+\sqrt{2n}.$$
So $p$ is a prime divisor of $n^2+1$ greater than $2n+\sqrt{2n}$.

**Infinitely many $n$.** Each $n$ has $n^2+1$ with only finitely many prime factors, and each of the infinitely many primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$, $p\ge29$, produces such an $n$ with $p\mid n^2+1$. Hence infinitely many different $n$ arise. ∎

imo-2008-04.title: Pointwise two choices, then no mixing
imo-2008-04.body:
**Both work.** For $f(x)=x$ both sides are equal trivially. For $f(x)=\frac1x$ the left side is $\dfrac{\frac{w^2+x^2}{w^2x^2}}{\frac{y^2+z^2}{y^2z^2}}=\dfrac{w^2+x^2}{y^2+z^2}$ because $wx=yz$.

**$f(t^2)=f(t)^2$, $f(1)=1$.** Take $w=x=y=z=t$: $\frac{2f(t)^2}{2f(t^2)}=1$. With $t=1$, $f(1)=f(1)^2$, so $f(1)=1$.

**$f(t)\in\{t,\frac1t\}$.** Take $w=t$, $x=1$, $y=z=\sqrt t$ (then $wx=yz$): $\dfrac{f(t)^2+1}{2f(t)}=\dfrac{t^2+1}{2t}$, i.e. $f(t)+\frac1{f(t)}=t+\frac1t$. This rearranges to $(f(t)-t)\left(1-\frac{1}{t f(t)}\right)=0$, so $f(t)=t$ or $f(t)=\frac1t$.

**No mixing.** Suppose $f(a)=a$ and $f(b)=\frac1b$ with $a\ne1$, $b\ne1$ (so these choices are genuinely different from the other option). Take $w=\sqrt a$, $x=\sqrt b$, $y=1$, $z=\sqrt{ab}$; using $f(t^2)=f(t)^2$,
$$\frac{a+\frac1b}{1+f(ab)}=\frac{a+b}{1+ab}.$$
- If $f(ab)=ab$: $a+\frac1b=a+b$, so $b=1$. Contradiction.
- If $f(ab)=\frac1{ab}$: the left side is $\frac{(a+\frac1b)ab}{ab+1}=\frac{a(ab+1)}{ab+1}=a$, so $a+b=a+a^2b$, $a^2=1$, $a=1$. Contradiction.

Hence either $f(t)=t$ for all $t$, or $f(t)=\frac1t$ for all $t$ (at $t=1$ both agree). ∎

imo-2008-05.title: A $2^{k-n}$-to-one map
imo-2008-05.body:
Record a sequence as a word of length $k$ over $\{1,\dots,2n\}$ (the lamp switched at each step). A word is counted by $N$ iff each lamp $1,\dots,n$ occurs an odd number of times and each lamp $n+1,\dots,2n$ an even number of times; it is counted by $M$ iff moreover lamps $n+1,\dots,2n$ do not occur at all.

$M>0$: switch lamps $1,\dots,n$ once each and then lamp $1$ another $k-n$ (even) times.

**The map.** For an $N$-word, replace every letter $n+i$ by $i$ ($1\le i\le n$). Lamp $i$ now occurs (odd)$+$(even) $=$ odd times and lamps $n+1,\dots,2n$ do not occur, so we get an $M$-word.

**Counting preimages.** Fix an $M$-word in which lamp $i$ occurs $c_i$ times ($c_i$ odd, $\sum c_i=k$). Its preimages are obtained by choosing, for each $i$, a set of positions among the $c_i$ occurrences of $i$ to change into $n+i$; the result is an $N$-word iff each chosen set has even size (then $n+i$ occurs evenly and $i$ still oddly often). A set of $c_i\ge1$ elements has $2^{c_i-1}$ subsets of even size. So the number of preimages is
$$\prod_{i=1}^n2^{c_i-1}=2^{k-n},$$
the same for every $M$-word. Hence $N=2^{k-n}M$.

**Answer:** $N/M=2^{k-n}$

imo-2008-06.title: Homotheties through the point of $\omega$ nearest $AC$ (official solution, reworded)
imo-2008-06.body:
**Lemma 1.** $AB+AD=CB+CD$.

*Proof.* Let $\omega$ touch lines $BA,BC,CD,DA$ at $K,L,M,N$; by hypothesis $K$ is beyond $A$ on ray $BA$ and $L$ beyond $C$ on ray $BC$, and $\omega$ touches the extensions of $AD$, $CD$ beyond $D$. Then $AB=BK-AK$, $AD=AN-DN$, $CB=BL-CL$, $CD=CM-DM$. Equal tangents give $BK=BL$, $AK=AN$, $CL=CM$, $DN=DM$, so $AB+AD=(BK-AK)+(AK-DN)=BK-DN$ and $CB+CD=BL-DM$ equal each other. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** Let the incircle of a triangle $XYZ$ touch $XZ$ at $U$, let $UU'$ be its diameter, and let line $YU'$ meet $XZ$ at $V$. Then $V$ is the point where the excircle opposite $Y$ touches $XZ$.

*Proof.* The tangent to the incircle at $U'$ is parallel to $XZ$ and cuts off a small triangle $X'YZ'$ similar to $XYZ$, for which the incircle of $XYZ$ is the excircle opposite $Y$, touching $X'Z'$ at $U'$. The homothety with centre $Y$ taking $X'Z'$ to $XZ$ takes this circle to the excircle of $XYZ$ opposite $Y$ and $U'$ to the point $V=YU'\cap XZ$. $\square$

Recall that if the incircle of $XYZ$ touches $XZ$ at $U$, the excircle opposite $Y$ touches $XZ$ at the point $V$ with $ZV=XU$.

**Main proof.** Let $\omega_1$ touch $AC$ at $P$ and $\omega_2$ touch $AC$ at $Q$. Then
$$AP=\frac{AC+AB-BC}{2},\qquad CQ=\frac{CA+CD-AD}{2},$$
and $AB-BC=CD-AD$ by Lemma 1, so $AP=CQ$. Hence $Q$ is the point where the excircle of $ABC$ opposite $B$ touches $AC$, and $P$ is the point where the excircle of $ADC$ opposite $D$ touches $AC$. Also $P\ne Q$, since $AP=AQ$ would mean $AB=BC$.

Let $PP'$ and $QQ'$ be the diameters of $\omega_1,\omega_2$ perpendicular to $AC$; $P'$ is on $B$'s side of $AC$, $Q'$ on $D$'s side. By Lemma 2, $B,P',Q$ are collinear and $D,Q',P$ are collinear.

The circle $\omega$ lies on the far side of $AC$ from $B$. Let $T$ be the point of $\omega$ closest to line $AC$ (the endpoint of its diameter perpendicular to $AC$ nearer to $AC$). Both $\omega_1$ and $\omega$ are inscribed in angle $ABC$, so a homothety with centre $B$ and positive ratio maps $\omega_1$ to $\omega$; it maps $P'$ (the point of $\omega_1$ with tangent parallel to $AC$ on $B$'s side) to $T$. So $B,P',T$ are collinear. Similarly $\omega_2$ is inscribed in angle $ADC$ and $\omega$ in its vertical angle, so a homothety with centre $D$ and negative ratio maps $\omega_2$ to $\omega$ and $Q'$ to $T$; so $D,Q',T$ are collinear.

Consequently $T$ lies on line $P'Q$ (the line $BP'$) and on line $Q'P$ (the line $DQ'$). Since $PP'\parallel QQ'$, the homothety with centre $T$ sending $P'$ to $Q$ sends line $PP'$ to line $QQ'$ and hence $P$ (on line $TQ'$) to $Q'$. It maps the diameter $P'P$ of $\omega_1$ onto the diameter $QQ'$ of $\omega_2$, so it maps $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$. The vectors $\overrightarrow{P'P}$ and $\overrightarrow{QQ'}$ both point from $B$'s side towards $D$'s side, so the ratio is positive (and $\ne1$, as a homothety with ratio $1$ has no centre).

So $T$ is the centre of the positive homothety between the non-congruent circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. These circles lie on opposite sides of $AC$, so they are disjoint and have two common external tangents, which pass through exactly this centre. Hence the external tangents meet at $T\in\omega$. ∎
